papers.title: ATTUNE: Agentic Throughput Tuning for LLM Training
papers.abstract: The throughput of an LLM training job depends on its recipe: how the model is split across GPUs, how memory is traded for compute, and which kernels and communication overlaps it uses. The best recipe changes with every model, accelerator and framework version. Automated tuners search a fixed space of knobs and check only that a job runs, so they miss levers outside that space and can ship a configuration that silently changes training. ATTUNE is a coding agent that tunes any working recipe unattended within a GPU-hour budget. Guided by a skill of search rules, scripts and lessons from past tuning campaigns, it diagnoses each run and changes one lever at a time. A correctness gate outside the agent refuses any argument known to change the training objective. ATTUNE tunes Amazon's production post-training recipes on H100, H200 and B200 clusters, raising throughput by 1.7x on average. It beats the published throughput of four of NVIDIA's own benchmark recipes on NVIDIA's AutoModel framework by 6-17%. On models held out from its development, it improves the strongest public recipes most where they were written for another setting, by up to 2.6x on MiniMax-M2, and least where the vendor tuned them for the same hardware. Given the same GPU-hour budget, it outperforms existing automated tuners, including Bayesian optimization, random search and OptiCo, a recent LLM-agent tuner. Its gain on GLM-4.5 is more than four times the best alternative's. The same coding agent without ATTUNE's skill gains less and fails half its launches. We release ATTUNE at https://github.com/amazon-science/attune and OpenRecipes, a leaderboard of tuned and verified training recipes, at https://openrecipes.ai.

deep_reading.content:
Before training a large model, engineers have to settle on a "training recipe": how the model is split across tens or hundreds of GPUs, how much computation to trade for memory when memory runs short, which low-level compute routines to use, and how data transfers between GPUs overlap with computation. Move the same model to a different GPU or framework version, and the recipe that used to be fastest often no longer is. Amazon built a system called ATTUNE that lets an AI agent able to write code and run commands tune recipes: give it a recipe that runs and a budget of GPU-hours, and it tries things, analyses bottlenecks and keeps going on its own, with no one watching. But the real point of the paper lies outside the agent: ==a "correctness gate" run by fixed code the agent cannot change, which rejects before launch any change that would quietly alter what is being trained==. After Amazon's fine-tuning jobs for three in-house models switched to the tuned recipes, training ran on average 1.7 times as fast as before, and up to 3.9 times.

![ATTUNE's structure: one agent works in a loop of "form a hypothesis, launch a trial, analyse where time goes, diagnose the bottleneck"; outside it, a gate written as fixed code rejects parameters that change what is trained, judges whether a measurement is valid and decides which recipe is currently fastest; an outer harness keeps it running unattended, a ledger records every run, and a lesson library passes past experience to the next tuning job.](figs/2610.17528/hf1.png)

## 1. The problem: existing auto-tuners either cannot find the answer or "break" the training

A training recipe has many "levers" that can be adjusted. The most important is how the model is split: each layer's matrices can be cut up across several cards, different layers can be given to different cards that pass work along like a pipeline, or the data can be split so that several groups of cards each compute one share. There is more: when memory is short, whether to discard intermediate results and recompute them when needed (trading compute for memory); whether to park some data in CPU memory; which version of the attention routine to use.

Existing auto-tuners fall roughly into three kinds. The first picks from a pre-listed set of options using a formula that estimates performance. The second is "black-box" search, such as Bayesian optimisation: it does not understand how the system works, it just runs trial after trial and decides what to try next from the results, but each trial is expensive. The third is the recent kind of large-model tuner, such as OptiCo, which can read performance analyses but likewise only adjusts a fixed list of knobs.

Two observations by the authors shaped ATTUNE's design.

First, part of the speed a stock recipe leaves on the table is hidden in combinations of levers that **only help when changed together**, and part in levers that the fixed list **does not include at all**, such as switching to a different routine for distributing data among cards.

Second, some settings quietly change what is being trained, while training still finishes without errors. Two examples. In "mixture-of-experts" models, each input word is sent to a few "expert" sub-networks. A common speed-up parameter caps how many words each expert handles, and words over the cap are simply dropped and not trained on. Another parameter, judging by its name, only "sends gradients at lower precision", but in fact it also makes gradient accumulation low-precision. A tuner that only checks "does it run" would hand both settings over as "optimisations", and the trained model would differ from the original.

## 2. Method: the agent searches, fixed code judges

One tuning job is called a "campaign": one fixed model, one cluster, a fixed number of GPUs. Every candidate recipe trains exactly the same thing: model, data, length of each example, examples per step and numeric precision stay the same, and every run even reads the same data in the same order. Each trial runs a fixed number of steps; the first few are warm-up and not scored, and after that the score is the average number of words each GPU processes per second.

Speed measurements are noisy, so first one has to decide "how much faster counts as really faster". The original recipe runs at least 5 times on different machines to get its average speed and its standard deviation as a share of that average, $\sigma$. The noise band is the larger of 3% and $3\sigma$; a new candidate must beat the current fastest by more than this band to replace it. That way a run that happened to be fast is not mistaken for a real improvement.

The agent uses only ordinary tools: reading and writing files (including the training framework's source code), running commands, and calling the cluster's interface. A written "tuning code of practice" sets it six rules; the three most important are:

- before every launch, write down a hypothesis: which bottleneck to ease, why it should work, and how much faster it should be;
- change only one lever at a time, or one set of splitting choices that must change together, so the result can be attributed;
- before using a parameter, read its implementation in the framework source to see whether it quietly changes other parameters too, and record the code location in the ledger.

When the bottleneck is unclear, the agent runs a performance analysis: a fixed analysis program splits each training step's time into computation, data transfer between GPUs, work on the CPU side, and idle waiting, telling the agent where time is mainly being wasted.

Spending is policed by fixed code. An accounting script counts from the moment the cluster allocates machines until they are released, including failed runs and runs used for checks, and nothing launches if the budget is not enough. Re-running a failed recipe unchanged is also refused, forcing the agent to find the cause before changing it.

The correctness gate has two steps, and it is the heart of the system.

The first step happens before launch: compare all parameters and environment variables that **finally take effect** in the candidate and in the original recipe. Final values are compared because one parameter may quietly change others. Every change is looked up in a register that the agent cannot edit. Changes that alter what is trained (data, examples per step, optimiser, loss function, routing, numeric precision), or that trigger known software defects, are rejected outright. Changes that alter only "how it is computed" and not "what is computed", such as a different way of placing data on GPUs, are passed outright. Anything not in the register is passed on to the second step and written into the report for a person to review.

The second step happens after launch: compare the loss at the first training step, i.e. how wrong the model is on the first batch of data. At the first step the weights have just been loaded and not yet updated, so the candidate and the original face the same weights and the same batch, and their losses should be almost identical. Legitimate changes only cause tiny differences from a different order of computation, whereas weights that were loaded or split wrongly make the loss change several-fold. So the rule is that the first-step loss must be within 5% of the original's, and no loss in the whole trial may be infinite or invalid.

To make it truly unattended, the authors added several hooks around Claude Code: the agent cannot finish until the budget is spent or it has written down a reason to stop, with evidence; when it wants to ask a person something, it instead "takes the default and records the assumption"; unknown destructive commands are blocked. Every run is written into an append-only ledger, so the system can recover even after a crash. When a campaign ends, the agent writes down lessons, which go into the lesson library for next time after human review.

## 3. Result one: faster than the strongest public recipes

The authors first reproduced NVIDIA's four official benchmark recipes unchanged on their own cluster; three came within 2% of NVIDIA's published speed, showing that the starting point was fair. From those recipes ATTUNE gained another 7% to 26%, putting it 6% to 17% above NVIDIA's published figures. The authors then took four models not seen during development and tuned them starting from public recipes written by others.

| Model | Hardware | Speed-up |
| --- | --- | ---: |
| Qwen3-30B-A3B | 8 H100s | +9.9% |
| GPT-OSS-20B | 8 H100s | +17.4% |
| Llama-3.1-70B | 64 H100s | +26.4% |
| GLM-4.5 | 128 B200s | +33.9% |
| MiniMax-M2 | 64 B200s | +164.2% |
| Llama-3.1-405B | 128 B200s | +6.8% |
| Mixtral-8x22B | 128 H100s | 0% (original kept) |

How much speed can be gained depends on how far the original recipe is from the current setting. MiniMax-M2's original recipe was written for reinforcement learning on 128 cards and kept the optimiser's data in CPU memory to save GPU memory; on 64 cards doing ordinary training, that trick slows things down instead. ATTUNE turned it off and changed how the pipeline was split, raising the speed to 2.6 times the original. GLM-4.5's recipe was written for H100s; on B200s the diagnosis found the bottleneck had become transferring data between machines and launching many small compute tasks. ATTUNE therefore shrank expert parallelism so that each expert group sits on the GPUs of one machine. Every token's experts are then local, and the data exchange between experts no longer crosses machines; the routing rule and the model are unchanged, only the placement of experts on GPUs. The fastest campaign also cut tensor parallelism to 1. Llama-3.1-70B switched to a faster attention routine, and computation came to take 98.5% of each step, with almost no idle waiting. The Mixtral and 405B recipes had already been tuned by the vendor for the same hardware, leaving little to gain; Mixtral's best candidate stayed within the noise, so by the rules the original recipe was kept.

## 4. Result two: with the same budget, it finds better recipes than other tuners

The authors gave every tuning method the same budget: 30 times the GPU-hours of one trial of the original recipe, with the same gate and the same release rules, and 3 campaigns per model. On GLM-4.5, ATTUNE gained 33.9% on average using only 669 GPU-hours and 6.4 hours; OptiCo gained nothing yet spent 1,407 GPU-hours; random search gained 7.8%; Bayesian optimisation only 1.8%. On MiniMax-M2, ATTUNE gained 164.2%, the best rival 55.5%. This shows ATTUNE not only found faster recipes but also spent less on the tuning itself.

![GLM-4.5, 128 B200s: how each tuning method's "best speed-up found so far" changes as GPU-hours are spent. ATTUNE passed 20% before using 30% of its budget, and stopped long before the budget was spent.](figs/2610.17528/hf2.png)

Most interesting is why OptiCo failed. The way of splitting the model that ATTUNE found on GLM-4.5 is actually within the 11 knobs OptiCo can adjust: rebuilt from those 11 knobs alone, it runs within 2% of ATTUNE's final recipe, but OptiCo did not find it: it only tried the relevant setting with shallower pipelines, and its data exchange between experts always crossed machines. The answer was inside the black-box search space, but without diagnosis to point the way, most attempts either ran out of memory or were slower than the current best and got discarded. This shows that ATTUNE's advantage comes mainly from "look at the bottleneck before acting", not merely from having more things it can change.

The authors also removed ATTUNE's parts one at a time to see the effect. Without the code of practice and lesson library, the speed-ups on the two test models fell from 88.0% to 66.9% and from 49.4% to 42.9%, and half the trials failed to launch properly. Allowed only OptiCo's 11 knobs, GLM-4.7-Flash got just 18.1%, because its biggest gain came from turning off "keep optimiser data in CPU memory", which is not on that list.

## 5. Can the gate itself be trusted

The authors tested the gate specifically. All 460 legitimate runs were passed, and every configuration error was rejected before launch. They then deliberately planted 6 kinds of errors in the code: the 2 that change the model's forward computation raised the first-step loss by over 150% and were caught. Errors that only act when weights are updated, such as leaving out part of the gradient summation, cannot be seen at the first step at all. Shifting the labels by one word when computing the loss changed it by only 2%, about the same as the largest legitimate difference. These slipped through.

The gate also proved its worth in real use. On Nemotron-3-Nano, the configuration check blocked 19 pipeline splits with "unequal numbers of layers per stage". One of them happened to be the fastest of all trials, but it loaded other layers' weights into the wrong layers, and its first-step loss was 215% to 768% higher than normal. Without the gate, this "fastest recipe" would have been handed over.

## 6. Limitations and practical meaning

The authors list three limitations. First, the gate only looks at the configuration and the first step, so errors that act only when weights are updated go unnoticed, and a full training run is still needed for validation before real use. Second, the lesson library comes from past tuning, and GLM-4.5 belongs to the same family as a model used during development, so some of the gain may come from "having seen something similar". Without the lesson library, however, GLM-4.5's result was within the noise of the full system. Third, ATTUNE only tunes configuration the framework exposes; it does not change low-level compute routines or code, and does not cover the part of reinforcement learning where the model generates samples. There is one more lesson: when the authors went back and checked the lesson library, about one fifth of the entries were wrong, some holding only for the job on which they were first measured.

For training-platform teams, the most useful parts to borrow are the gate and the accounting, not the agent itself. Whether tuning is done by a person or an agent, you can first build a set of checks: compare the parameters that finally take effect, look them up in an uneditable register of "changes that alter what is trained", then compare the first-step loss. That keeps parameters which quietly change training, like "drop words over the cap" or "accumulate gradients at low precision", out before launch. Budgets should count from machine allocation to release, failed runs included. If your recipe was carried over from other hardware or another task (such as reinforcement learning), auto-tuning pays off most; if you use a vendor recipe tuned for the same hardware, expect much less, as in the paper such recipes gained only 0% to 26%. The lesson library should be checked against the original records regularly, keeping only entries the model does not already know or that correct its wrong intuitions.

papers.title: uGDS: A User-Space Development Kit for High-Performance GPU Direct Storage
papers.abstract: Data-intensive GPU applications increasingly rely on NVMe SSDs to extend GPU memory. NVIDIA GPU Direct Storage (GDS) enables direct SSD-GPU transfers via PCIe peer-to-peer DMA, eliminating host staging. However, GDS retains three key limitations: (1) its control path traverses the kernel for every I/O request, introducing software overhead; (2) its stream-ordered path imposes strict total ordering even when workloads only require batch-level ordering; and (3) its closed-source user-space engine hinders diagnosis and custom scheduling. We present uGDS, https://github.com/ScaleX-IO/uGDS, an open-source user-space GPU Direct Storage library built on four principles: user-space control, unified cross-vendor abstraction, workload-aware scheduling, and end-to-end transparency. The host CPU manages the entire NVMe command lifecycle in user space, while payloads move via PCIe P2P DMA without consuming GPU compute. A minimal kernel module (ugds_drv.ko) is used only for one-time privileged setup. uGDS partitions hardware queues between synchronous and batch traffic, enforces DMA-safe buffer lifetimes, and provides cuFile-compatible synchronous, batched, and stream-ordered APIs with polling or interrupt completion on both NVIDIA CUDA and AMD HIP. deep_reading.title: uGDS: A User-Space Development Kit for High-Performance GPU Direct Storage
deep_reading.content:
Large-model inference services store the KV cache they have already computed on SSDs, so that the next request with the same opening can read them back instead of recomputing. NVIDIA provides GPU Direct Storage (GDS for short below) for this, letting data go from SSD straight into GPU memory without a stop in host memory. Yet when the authors measured it inside the open-source cache system LMCache, asynchronous reads through GDS on a single task queue reached only 2.36 GiB/s, less than half of synchronous read bandwidth; 99.6% of the time was stuck at the "submit request" step. This paper from Sun Yat-sen University, HKUST (Guangzhou) and others open-sources uGDS, which moves the job of "telling the SSD what to do" out of the operating-system kernel and into an ordinary program. ==Data still goes straight from SSD to GPU; what changes is who gives the orders==. On one A100 GPU plus one Samsung 990 PRO SSD, uGDS's batched reads are up to 12 times as fast as GDS and batched writes up to 30 times; plugged into LMCache, the median time-to-first-token for long prompts (from sending a request to seeing the first output word) fell from 1.9 seconds to 0.7 seconds.

![uGDS's three paths: privileged setup done once at start-up is handed to a small kernel module; in normal operation, issuing commands to the SSD, notifying it to start and collecting its completion reports are all done by the CPU in an ordinary program; data moves directly between the SSD and GPU memory without passing through host memory.](figs/2610.30868/hf1.png)

## 1. The problem: data no longer takes a detour, but commands still do

First, the difference between the "data path" and the "control path". The data path is where the data itself flows from and to; the control path is who tells the hardware, and through which steps, "move this piece of data to that place".

GDS fixed the data path: an SSD can DMA data over PCIe straight into GPU memory, without the CPU copying it. But GDS's control path enters the operating-system kernel every time: a read request passes in turn through the virtual file system, the actual file system, the block-device layer and the kernel's SSD driver, and NVIDIA's kernel module also looks up a GPU address for every 4 KiB page of data. When moving one large block, these fixed costs are spread thin and hardly noticed; but in KV cache reads and writes and vector search, requests tend to be small, frequent and latency-sensitive, and these costs become the main expense.

The authors point to two further problems with GDS.

First, **the queueing rules are too rigid**. GDS's asynchronous interface inherits the rule of GPU task queues (CUDA streams): within one queue, every request waits for the previous one to finish. But when LMCache reads back a stretch of cache, the small pieces need no particular order; they only have to all arrive before the model's computation begins. To use the full bandwidth, applications have to spread requests over many queues, effectively doing GDS's scheduling for it.

Second, **problems are invisible**. GDS's kernel part is open source, but the user-space library that handles batched submission, background threads and queue integration is released only as a binary. When things stall you can neither find the cause nor change the policy.

Others had already driven SSDs directly from ordinary programs, showing that this path works, but those prototypes supported only NVIDIA GPUs, assumed a single submitting thread, and did not track "requests still in flight", so a program could free a piece of GPU memory while the SSD was still writing into it.

## 2. Method: the CPU gives commands, the SSD moves data, the GPU only computes

uGDS separates three things.

At start-up, privileged setup is done once, by a small kernel module: it takes the SSD over from the kernel driver, maps the SSD's control registers and command queues into memory the program can read and write directly, locks the GPU memory to be used, and records its addresses on the bus.

During normal reads and writes the kernel is not involved at all. Following the SSD's protocol (NVMe, the standard command format for solid-state drives), the program itself writes a 64-byte command saying where on the disk to read, how much, and which pages of GPU memory to put it in. It then writes a number into a "doorbell" register on the SSD to signal a new command. After that it checks the completion queue for the SSD's report that it is done. The whole process is ordinary memory reads and writes, with no system calls.

The data itself still moves directly between the SSD and GPU memory, not through host memory.

The cost is that the SSD must be detached from the kernel driver and given to uGDS exclusively, and the program sees "byte number such-and-such on the disk" rather than files. The authors argue this fits cache engines like LMCache and Mooncake, which manage their own storage blocks; if files are needed, a user-space file system can be layered on top.

To make this path both fast and safe, uGDS has four designs.

First, **it supports both NVIDIA and AMD GPUs**. When GPU memory is registered, each vendor's memory addresses are translated into a uniform list of page addresses the SSD understands, so code above does not need to know whose card it is.

Second, **command queues are split into two groups**. SSDs support several sets of command queues. uGDS sets aside one deep queue just for batched requests, and the rest serve single synchronous requests. That way, when a large batch floods in, single requests are not left waiting behind it. Batched requests also gather many commands and ring the "doorbell" only once, saving repeated notification costs.

Third, **it prevents "freeing while writing"**. This is where driving hardware yourself most easily goes wrong. For each request sent, uGDS notes "transfer in flight" against the GPU memory involved; trying to free that memory while a transfer is in flight is refused outright. Each registration also carries an increasing number, so that an old request cannot hit newly allocated memory that reuses the same address. If a command times out, the disk is marked faulty and isolated, and resources can only be reclaimed after a hardware reset confirms the SSD has stopped.

Fourth, **completion notification is selectable**. By default the CPU keeps polling the completion queue, which responds fastest but occupies a whole CPU core. Hardware interrupts can be used instead, with the kernel only waking the program and everything else still done in user space.

None of these ideas is new on its own: SPDK, which drives SSDs directly from ordinary programs, has long existed. uGDS's contribution is turning them into **a GPU storage library that maps one-to-one onto GDS's interface and can be swapped in for production use**: it has synchronous, batched and queue-ordered asynchronous interfaces, both vendors' GPUs share one abstraction, the safety mechanisms are in place, and everything from the kernel module to user space is open source. ==The most practical point is that a single queue can use the full bandwidth, so applications no longer need to split requests over a dozen queues==.

## 3. Experiments: small requests, batched requests and the first batch

Tests used a server with two Intel Xeon CPUs, one A100 GPU and one Samsung 990 PRO 1TB SSD, compared against NVIDIA's current version of GDS.

uGDS starts faster: median initialisation is 42 milliseconds, against 115 for GDS, which spends almost all of it opening NVIDIA's driver session, loading configuration and probing the bus topology. For elastic services that frequently start and retire worker processes, this saves a fair amount of time.

Single small requests gain the most. With 2 threads writing 4 KiB blocks, uGDS's bandwidth is 6.2 times GDS's and average latency falls from 48 microseconds to 7.7, because each request skips a long chain of kernel steps. With more threads and bigger requests, the bottleneck moves to the SSD and the bus themselves, and the gap narrows to 1.2 to 1.4 times. On an AMD platform, against AMD's equivalent library, it is also about 1.2 times as fast.

Batched requests lead across the board. The authors tested 36 combinations of "request size × requests per batch", and uGDS won all of them: reads 2.1 to 12.1 times GDS, writes 2.3 to 30.7 times. The smaller the requests and the more per batch, the bigger the gap.

![Batched read bandwidth as request size and requests per batch vary; the number in each cell is how many times faster uGDS is than GDS. The gap is largest with small requests and large batches.](figs/2610.30868/hf8.png)

Following an anomaly, the authors tracked down a problem in GDS. More requests per batch should mean faster, yet for 128 KiB writes GDS got slower as batches grew. The cause is the first batch: with 128 requests per batch, GDS's first batch takes 91 milliseconds to read and 118 to write, nearly ninety percent of the whole 64 MiB transfer time. This is because GDS defers mapping GPU memory addresses until the first read or write, and the authors suspect it also allocates the internal state needed for batching only at the first submission. uGDS does all this during initialisation, so its first batch is almost as fast as later ones. Even leaving out the first batch and looking only at the steady state, with 4 KiB requests and 128 per batch, uGDS still reads 8.8 times and writes 23.8 times as fast as GDS.

Polling and interrupts each have their uses. For small 4 KiB requests, constant CPU polling cuts latency from 21 microseconds to 9, at the cost of a fully busy core. For large 1 MiB requests, switching to interrupts lowers the CPU use of the requesting thread from 100% to 4%, with only 5.5% more latency. So polling suits latency-sensitive cases, and interrupts are better value for large transfers.

## 4. Real-world effect: inside LMCache

The authors plugged uGDS into LMCache and ran end-to-end tests with the small Qwen3-0.6B model and the vLLM inference framework. To test the SSD path specifically, they turned off vLLM's own in-memory cache, so every cache hit had to be read back from the SSD.

| Metric | GDS | uGDS |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Median time-to-first-token, 32,768-token long prompt | 1915 ms | 715 ms |
| Throughput, 1,024-token short requests, 256 concurrent | about 19,000 tokens/s (tops out at 32 concurrent) | 50,000 tokens/s |
| Share of total time spent on "submit request" | 99.6% | 1.0% |
| Single-queue asynchronous read bandwidth | 2.36 GiB/s | 5.49 GiB/s |

For prompts from 3,840 to 40,704 tokens, uGDS's time-to-first-token is consistently about four tenths of GDS's. The time for the GPU to place the read-back data into vLLM's memory is the same on both sides, which shows that all of the saving comes from the storage path. Another key difference is scaling: GDS tops out at around 32 concurrent requests, while uGDS keeps scaling to 256, with 2.6 times GDS's throughput.

![LMCache reading all cache from SSD: the left panel shows median time-to-first-token as prompt length grows, the right panel shows throughput for short requests as concurrency grows; GDS tops out near 32 concurrent requests, while uGDS keeps rising to 256.](figs/2610.30868/hf14.png)

## 5. Limitations

uGDS must have the whole SSD to itself: once detached from the kernel driver, the disk has no file system and cannot be used as an ordinary disk by other programs. Currently one uGDS instance drives only one local SSD; using several disks together and reaching remote SSDs over a network are still planned. Synchronous requests are assigned to command queues in turn and hold the queue until done, so a large request slows small ones on the same queue; the authors plan a load-aware scheduler. The experiments used only one consumer SSD and one A100, with the IOMMU (the hardware that checks addresses when devices access memory) turned off, and the end-to-end test used only a small 0.6B model. How it performs with data-centre SSDs, and with several GPUs sharing a bus switch chip, remains to be verified.

## 6. Practical meaning

If you work on tiered KV cache storage (GPU memory, host memory and SSD) or GPU vector search, and the SSD is a dedicated local disk, uGDS is worth trying as a replacement for GDS. Small, frequent reads on a single queue are exactly where GDS suffers most and uGDS gains most.

Before going live, confirm three things: whether the SSD can be dedicated and detached from the kernel driver; whether the layer above already manages its own storage-block allocation, as LMCache and Mooncake do; and whether the server's IOMMU settings allow the SSD and GPU to transfer directly. When deploying, pick the completion method by workload: CPU polling for latency-sensitive inference nodes, interrupts for throughput-oriented or CPU-constrained jobs.

Even without switching libraries, two of the paper's findings about GDS apply directly. First, GDS spends tens of extra milliseconds preparing the first time it reads or writes a piece of GPU memory, so after a service starts it should do one warm-up read or write for each "GPU memory and disk" pair. Second, GDS's single queue gets blocked on submission, so critical reads should be split across several queues in parallel.

papers.title: RACE: RoPE-Aligned Attention Compression Based on Query-Key Activation Energies
papers.abstract: Head-dimension compression can reduce the memory required by the key-value (KV) cache, but existing methods often reconstruct full-dimensional representations during inference, adding significant decoding FLOPs overhead. We formalize the design considerations for converting pretrained attention into a natively reduced-dimensional form that reduces both KV-cache storage and attention computation using a calibration set. Specifically, we consider reductions that (1) apply a shared projection to queries and keys so that they remain in a common reduced feature space, (2) derive this projection jointly from query and key activations to better preserve their interaction, and (3) are compatible with the pretrained RoPE transformation. To obtain a reconstruction-free realization of this reduction, we restrict it to coordinate selection and theoretically show that RoPE compatibility then holds if and only if complete rotary pairs are retained. Building on this characterization, we introduce RACE, a post-training method that selects rotary pairs using their joint query-key activation energy. We theoretically show that this criterion minimizes a separable, calibration-dependent upper bound on post-RoPE query-key product approximation error. The resulting reductions are folded into the model weights and require neither runtime reconstruction nor specialized kernels. Across three model families and different compression levels, RACE outperforms structured pruning and remains competitive with reconstruction-based methods on language-modeling, zero-shot, and long-context tasks. At 50% KV-cache retention and 256K context, RACE reduces total inference FLOPs by 47.8%, yielding 1.79x higher throughput, 43.2% lower time-to-first-token (TTFT), and 28.1% lower allocated GPU memory in comparison to an uncompressed model.

The pairs kept are those where queries and keys have the largest sum of squares on a small batch of text, and that choice is written directly into the model weights. On Llama-3.2-3B, with vectors halved and an input of 256,000 tokens, overall throughput rises to 1.79 times and time-to-first-token falls 43.2%.

deep_reading.title: RACE: RoPE-Aligned Attention Compression Based on Query-Key Activation Energies
deep_reading.content:
When a large model processes long text, it has to keep the intermediate results left by every word it has read in GPU memory; this "memory" is called the KV cache. The longer the text, the bigger it gets, and at a few hundred thousand words it often takes more room than the model itself. There are three ways to compress it: store fewer words, lower the precision of each number, or make the vector stored for each word shorter. Methods for the third way exist, but most only save storage: they store short vectors, yet at compute time must first restore them to full length, so computation balloons, up to 22 times the original. This paper's RACE (RoPE-Aligned Attention Compression) finds a way to shorten vectors **without restoring them**: ==keep only whole pairs of the coordinates the model's position encoding uses, then write that choice directly into the model weights==. That way storage, position encoding and attention computation all happen on the short vectors, with no change to the inference program. On Llama-3.2-3B, with vectors halved and an input of 256,000 tokens, total computation drops 47.8%, overall throughput rises to 1.79 times, and time-to-first-token falls 43.2%.

![Left: RACE shortens vectors before position encoding is applied and folds this step into the model weights, so attention runs on short vectors throughout. Right: the earlier approach stores short vectors in the cache but must restore them to full length with two matrices before every computation (the dashed boxes are computations at full length).](figs/2610.28385/hf2.png)

## 1. The problem: storage saved, computation not

First, some background knowledge. In the attention mechanism each word produces a "query" vector and a "key" vector; their dot product decides how much a word should attend to each earlier word. The KV cache stores the "key" and "value" vectors of every earlier word. The length of these vectors within each attention head is called the "head dimension", commonly 128. Cut the head dimension from 128 to 64 and the KV cache halves.

The difficulty is position encoding. Most models today use RoPE: every two adjacent numbers in a vector form a pair, which is rotated by an angle set by the word's position. The paper calls each such pair of coordinates a "rotation pair".

The problem is that if a general matrix is used to compress the key vector, the compression and the rotation cannot swap order: compressing then rotating gives a different result from rotating then compressing. And the model was trained with "rotate first". So EigenAttention and PALU (two methods that compress vectors with a matrix) have to restore the short vector to 128 dimensions before every computation, then rotate. Storage is saved, but computation gains an extra restoring step. By the paper's count, with storage halved, the computation to generate each new word is 11 times the original for EigenAttention and 22 times for PALU.

Two other existing approaches each miss a piece. Thin Keys needs no restoring, but compresses only key vectors and leaves value vectors alone, so the KV cache can only shrink to 75%. The concurrent RAP (a structured pruning method) also keeps whole rotation pairs, but decides which to keep by computing gradients, which needs back-propagation, and looks only at the key side.

## 2. Method: keep coordinates in pairs, choose them by "energy"

The authors state the goal clearly: find a way to shorten vectors so that the dot product of a short query and a short key comes as close as possible to that of the original long vectors, while the shortening can be done before rotation. Two principles follow. First, queries and keys must be shortened the same way, because a dot product multiplies the two vectors coordinate by coordinate and adds up, so the coordinates on both sides must line up. Second, choosing which coordinates to keep must look at both queries and keys, because what is being approximated is their product.

Which kind of shortening can be placed before rotation? The paper proves an exact condition. If the shortening simply picks out some coordinates and drops the rest, then it can swap order with rotation if and only if the coordinates picked are exactly a number of **whole rotation pairs**, in unchanged order. The reason is intuitive: the two coordinates of a pair mix with each other when rotated, so keeping only one loses the part the other mixed in. As long as pairs are kept whole, rotating the short vector by the original angles gives exactly the same result as "rotate everything, then pick coordinates".

Next, which pairs to keep. The authors run the model once over a small batch of general text, record how large the query and key values are on each rotation pair, and add up the squares of both sides as that pair's "energy". High energy means the pair contributes a lot to the dot product. To compress 128 dimensions to 64, keep the 32 pairs with the most energy. The authors prove that the error from dropping some pairs cannot exceed half the total energy of the dropped pairs. So choosing by energy exactly minimises this error bound. The authors also note that this is not the same as minimising the actual error; it is a practical criterion that needs only one forward pass and is very cheap to compute.

Value vectors are not rotated, so compressing them has no such restriction. The authors follow EigenAttention: from the same data, find the 64 directions in which value vectors vary most and keep only the components along them.

The last step "folds" these choices into the weights. Picking coordinates and finding directions both amount to multiplying by a fixed matrix, which can be multiplied in advance into the weight matrices that produce queries, keys and values, and into the final output matrix. The result is an ordinary attention layer whose head dimension has gone from 128 to 64. Position encoding is applied only to the kept rotation pairs, each still with its original rotation speed. The dot products and weighted sums that follow are all computed in 64 dimensions, and standard PyTorch attention runs it with no specially written low-level code.

When compression is aggressive, an optional "recovery training" step can follow: using 1 million tokens of general text, the compressed model learns to imitate the original model's outputs, updating only the changed attention weights and leaving everything else fixed. At 75% kept this step helps little; at 50% kept it recovers most of the lost quality.

The paper's core contribution is spelling out "which compressions are legal". Once it is proven that only the "keep pairs whole" family can work directly on short vectors, ==the question changes from "how to restore" to "which of the legal rotation pairs to pick"==. The compressed model is just a standard model with a smaller head dimension, and existing inference frameworks need no changes at all.

## 3. Experiment one: can quality keep up with methods that restore

| Method | Needs restoring | KV cache kept | Computation to read the prompt | Computation per generated word |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| EigenAttention | yes | 50% | 0.75 | 11.42 |
| PALU | yes | 50% | 0.75 | 21.92 |
| Thin Keys | no | 75% | 0.75 | 0.75 |
| RAP | no | 50% | 0.5 | 0.5 |
| RACE | no | 50% | 0.5 | 0.5 |

RACE's accuracy is close to the methods that restore, while its computation is as low as RAP's; the restoring methods need an order of magnitude more.](figs/2610.28385/hf1.png)

## 4. Experiment two: does the saved storage turn into real speed

Saving storage does not guarantee running faster, so the authors measured speed on Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct. Prompt lengths were 64,000, 128,000 and 256,000 tokens, each producing 128 output tokens, averaged over 10 runs per setting.

The longer the prompt, the bigger the gain, because with longer text attention takes a larger share of total computation. At 256,000 tokens and 50% kept, reading the prompt became 1.76 times as fast, generating word by word 1.90 times as fast, and overall throughput 1.79 times. GPU memory fell only 28%, not by half, because memory also holds the model's parameters and other intermediate results, which are unaffected.

At 50% kept, the gains are largest on the longest prompts.](figs/2610.28385/hf11.png)

The authors also tried stacking RACE with other compression: first RACE keeping 75%, then H2O or SnapKV dropping half the words, or KIVI (a method that lowers the numeric precision of the KV cache) halving precision, leaving 37.5% in total. Of the three combinations, stacking with KIVI's lower precision lost least, with especially stable perplexity.

Three more findings are useful. First, the text used to compute "energy" need not resemble the downstream task: between general text and task data, most tasks' scores differ by less than 6%. Third, the authors trained three small models of about 245 million parameters from scratch, with the same total dimension but different numbers and widths of heads. Under heavy compression, the model with fewer, wider heads held up best, because each head has more rotation pairs to choose from.

The authors point out several themselves. Choosing by energy minimises an upper bound on the error, not the actual error. Compressing to 50% needs one round of recovery training, so it is not fully training-free. When stacked with word-dropping methods, the losses of the two compression stages amplify each other. The paper's proof covers only the "pick coordinates directly" family of shortening; to avoid restoring, it deliberately gives up more general compression matrices, and it does not discuss whether something better exists in a wider family. Speed was measured on only one 3-billion-parameter model, and gains are smaller for prompts shorter than 256,000 tokens; the paper gives no results for larger models or for architectures where several query heads share one set of keys and values.

## 6. Practical meaning

For long-text inference services, RACE's biggest advantage is easy deployment: the output is a standard model file with a smaller head dimension, frameworks such as vLLM and SGLang need no low-level changes, and it can be stacked with lower-precision methods such as KIVI. papers.title: Cache Engineering for Agents
papers.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents can handle increasingly complex tasks, navigating long trajectories of observations and actions. As these trajectories grow, key-value (KV) cache I/O and storage become the dominant cost. Trajectories can also exceed the LLM's maximum context length, requiring control over active cache growth. Prior work uses context engineering to reduce cache size by trimming or summarizing history. However, modifying the trajectory prefix invalidates subsequent cached states and triggers costly re-prefilling of retained context. Task accuracy can also suffer when too little context is retained to limit re-prefill costs. We propose cache engineering as a new scheme. It allows agents to directly control their active KV cache without modifying the trajectory or re-prefilling retained context. Specifically, agents can proactively use drop to exclude selected cache from future attention and repos to adjust retained keys' position encodings. We formalize these cache operations and identify history dependence as a serving challenge: identical token sequences can yield different cache states under different cache operation sequences, making prefix matching insufficient for correct cache reuse. Thus, we co-design the AKV serving engine. It provides a stateless interface compatible with existing serving APIs, while internally managing stateful cache reuse, eviction, and restoration. Experiments show that a tool-response rolling-drop cache policy improves average benchmark scores by 1.7 points and reduces average cost by 27.7%, compared with conventional threshold-triggered summarization. With AKV, it achieves up to 1.2x the output throughput and a 1.5x speedup in P95 request latency. Recursive self-improvement of cache policies further reduces cost by 7.1% over expert design. Our code is at https://github.com/thu-nics/AKV.

papers.summary: When an agent goes back and forth with tools such as search, web pages and code execution for hundreds of turns, it pays a recurring cost. On every turn the model re-reads the KV cache of everything that came before, and reading this old cache accounts for 82.4% of total inference cost. The usual way to save money is to delete or summarize old messages, but any edit to earlier text invalidates all the cache after it, so everything from the edit point onward has to be recomputed. The authors work at a different layer: leave the text history untouched and drop only selected entries from the cache, while the remaining entries are reused as they are. A simple policy of keeping the cache of only the 12 most recent tool outputs beats the common approach of summarizing at the length limit, with a pass rate 1.7 percentage points higher on average across four agent benchmarks and 27.7% lower average cost.

deep_reading.content:
An agent working on a hard task often goes back and forth with tools such as search, web pages and code execution for hundreds of turns. On every turn the model re-reads the KV cache of everything that came before. The paper measures that reading this old cache accounts for 82.4% of total inference cost, far more than generating new tokens. The usual way to save money is to delete or summarize old messages, but any edit to earlier text invalidates all the cache after it, so everything from the edit point onward has to be recomputed. A Tsinghua team proposes working at a different layer: **leave the text history untouched and drop only selected entries from the cache**, while the remaining entries are reused as they are. They built an inference serving system for this, called AKV. Across three models and four agent benchmarks, a simple policy of "keep the cache of only the 12 most recent tool outputs" beats the common "summarize when the length limit is reached" approach, with ==a 1.7-point higher average score and 27.7% lower average cost==.

![Three approaches compared. Full: every turn reuses the whole history cache. Text editing: after irrelevant text is removed, the retained history must be recomputed. Cache editing: the text history stays the same and only selected cache entries are dropped; the rest need no recomputation. The nested color blocks show that the retained cache can still carry the influence of dropped content.](figs/2610.28577/hf1.png)

## 1. The problem: recomputation is expensive, and cutting everything at once loses information

The longer an agent's conversation gets, the more trouble the cache causes. The first problem is cost: the cache keeps growing and is read on every turn, so storing and reading it is expensive. The second is accuracy: a model can only handle so much context reliably, and once the content taking part in computation goes past that range, quality drops noticeably.

The standard fix today is to edit the text, also called "context engineering": delete old messages or replace them with summaries. But an LLM's cache is computed in order, and each token's cache depends on everything before it. The earlier the edit, the longer the stretch that must be recomputed. So common agent frameworks wait until the length hits some limit and then summarize most of the history in one go, keeping only the last few turns, which keeps the number of recomputations low. Cutting everything at once like this easily throws away useful information from the middle turns too.

The authors start with a comparison. They run GPT-OSS-120B on the first 100 questions of BrowseComp-Plus (a QA benchmark that needs many rounds of search to answer), 4 attempts per question with at most 100 turns. Keeping only the 12 most recent tool outputs by deleting text every turn costs 1.85 times as much as doing nothing, because of repeated recomputation. Summarizing once at 48K tokens cuts cost by only about 7% and drops accuracy by 5 points. Dropping old tool outputs directly from the cache improves accuracy and cost at the same time.

## 2. Method: three operations on the cache

The authors first separate two lengths. One is how long the conversation is as text. The other is how much cache actually takes part in later computation, which the paper calls the "active cache". Text editing changes the first; cache editing changes only the second.

In this framing, the paper defines three operations:

- **Append**: the normal case. Read in new tokens, attach their cache at the end, and increment the position index.
- **Drop**: exclude specified cache entries from all later computation. The remaining entries stay exactly as they are, the text history is unchanged, and new tokens keep counting positions upward as usual.
- **Reposition**: renumber the retained entries 0, 1, 2… in their original order, and number the next new token after them.

Why is the third operation needed? Dropping does not make the position indices smaller. The cache shrinks, but the index keeps climbing and will eventually exceed the largest position the model can handle. Repositioning pulls the indices back down. For models that use RoPE this step is cheap: to move an entry from position p to position q, rotate its key by the angle for q−p; the value stays the same and nothing is recomputed.

What gets dropped? The authors looked at the model's attention distribution and found two patterns: older content receives less attention, and at similar distances tool outputs receive less attention than the model's own reasoning. So the main policy is **rolling drop of old tool outputs**: keep all reasoning content and the 12 most recent tool outputs, and drop the cache of earlier tool outputs step by step.

## 3. The difficulty: the same text can have different caches

In a normal inference server, the same text prefix means the same cache, so caches can be reused by matching prefixes. Cache editing breaks this: **the same text, reached through a different order of operations, yields a different cache**.

![(a) Three operation sequences: ① append C after A and B, then drop A; ② drop A first, then append C; ③ start with only B, then append C. All three end with only B and C. (b) B's cache is the same in ① and ② but different in ③; C's cache differs in all three. (c) The improved cache index tree lets ① and ② share the A–B segment and branch on when A was dropped.](figs/2610.28577/hf5.png)

Take the example in the figure. All three paths end with only B and C kept. But in ①, C was computed while A was still visible, so it carries A's influence. In ②, A had already been dropped when C was computed. In ③, there was no A before B even when B itself was computed. So C's cache differs across the three paths. The paper therefore describes a cache state by "the full sequence of operations applied since an empty cache": for a given model, that sequence uniquely determines the current cache. The inference server has to remember both the text history and the operation history to reuse cache correctly.

## 4. AKV: turning this into an inference service

AKV's interface is almost identical to a standard chat API. The client sends the full message list as usual, with one extra optional field that says "after message N, drop these entries and reposition here". The client does not need to know which caches the server still holds; each turn it just appends messages and operations as usual.

Inside the server there are three mechanisms.

The first is **reuse**. Inference servers usually do prefix caching with a radix tree, so requests with the same prefix share a segment of cache. AKV adds "drop" and "reposition" nodes to the tree and matches on both text and operations during lookup. That is why ① and ② in the figure can share the A–B segment, while each keeps its own copy of C because A was dropped at different times.

The second is **reclamation**. A cache entry can be freed only when no in-flight computation still needs it. For example, once both ① and ② have dropped A, A's cache can be freed without waiting for the requests to finish. When GPU memory is tight, the server first reclaims cache that has been dropped and only then cache from finished requests, because the latter is more likely to be needed next turn.

The third is **recovery**. Once cache has been evicted from GPU memory, it has to be recomputed the next time it is needed. But a normal recompute from scratch can only produce the cache of "nothing ever dropped", and replaying each operation step by step would take many passes. AKV instead splits the content to be recomputed, at each layer, into segments at the drop and reposition points. Each segment attends only to itself and to the cache that earlier segments still retained at that time, and all segments are computed in one pass. This way a single computation restores the exact state after the drops and repositions.

## 5. Results

The baselines are two "summarize at the limit" approaches. The "standard" approach uses each model's own higher limit (96K tokens for GPT-OSS-120B and MiniMax-M2.7, 192K for MiroThinker-1.7-Mini). The "text editing" approach uses the same summarization but lowers the limit to 48K for all models. AKV uses rolling drop with "keep the 12 most recent tool outputs". There are four benchmarks: two multi-round search QA sets (BrowseComp-Plus, xbench-DeepSearch), the 103 text-only questions of GAIA, and SWE-bench Verified, which fixes bugs in real code repositories. Cost is priced on tokens actually read and generated. To avoid favoring their own method, the authors also charge every token touched by repositioning at the cache-read price, deliberately overestimating the cost of that step.

**Average over the four benchmarks (score is pass rate %, cost is cents per task):**

| Model | Standard | Text editing | AKV |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| MiniMax-M2.7 | 52.4 pts / 5.0 cents | 52.8 / 5.7 | 53.7 / 4.4 |
| GPT-OSS-120B | 51.0 / 11.2 | 48.3 / 10.2 | 53.1 / 7.3 |
| MiroThinker-1.7-Mini | 44.1 / 20.4 | 37.1 / 18.1 | 45.8 / 14.8 |

On all three models AKV has the highest average score, and its average cost is 27.7% lower than the standard approach and 21.9% lower than text editing. It does not win every cell, though: on MiniMax-M2.7, text editing scores higher on BrowseComp-Plus, and the standard approach is slightly higher on SWE-bench.

Why does accuracy improve? The authors break the results down by conversation length. Below 48K tokens the three approaches are about the same; between 48K and 96K, text editing is worst; above 96K, the standard approach is worst. These are exactly the points where each one triggers summarization, which shows that the lost points come from information thrown away by cutting everything at once. Rolling drop removes the oldest tool outputs a little at a time, so it avoids this problem.

On speed, the authors measure serving efficiency on SWE-bench with 8 A800 GPUs. At the highest concurrency each system can sustain, AKV's average latency is 1.36 times faster, the slowest 5% of requests are 1.51 times faster, and output throughput is 1.18 times that of the standard approach. The gap widens as concurrency goes up: the standard approach runs short of GPU memory and keeps evicting and recomputing cache, so at concurrency 16 the slowest 5% of requests wait 230 seconds, versus 31 seconds for AKV.

![GPT-OSS-120B on SWE-bench Verified: (a) cumulative pass rate on the first 100 tasks versus GPU hours spent; AKV reaches the highest pass rate with the least GPU time; (b) cumulative pass rate on 500 tasks versus cumulative tokens read; (c) serving throughput versus concurrency.](figs/2610.28577/hf8.png)

Several ablations are also useful. Dropping without repositioning scores 55.0 on BrowseComp-Plus; adding repositioning raises it to 62.0, because the agent can keep searching instead of hitting the position limit and being forced to stop. Dropping the cache of reasoning content, alone or together with tool outputs, is worse than dropping only tool outputs. The authors also tried letting the agent decide what to drop, and two models reached 61.0% and 64.0% on a subset of BrowseComp-Plus, which suggests the policy itself still has a lot of room to explore.

## 6. Limitations and practical value

The limitations the authors list: what to drop and when still needs more exploration; agents have not yet been trained specifically under this mechanism; and models with newer architectures such as linear attention are not supported. A few other points are worth noting. The main policy in the experiments is a fixed hand-written rule, and the best "how many to keep" may vary by task. Dropped content still leaves an indirect influence through cache computed afterwards. The authors see this as a strength, but it also means results depend on the order of operations, so debugging and reproduction require recording the full operation sequence.

For teams building agent platforms and inference services, the value of this paper is that it moves "context compression" from the text layer to the cache layer. Suppose your agent produces a lot of tool output, such as retrieval results, web pages or code execution output, and you currently control length by "summarize at the limit". First check on your own trajectories how much the model's attention to tool outputs differs from its attention to reasoning content. Then try "rolling drop of old tool outputs + repositioning", the most robust combination in the paper. ==The prerequisite for deployment is a serving layer that can tell operation histories apart==: if the server reuses cache only by matching text prefixes, different drop times under the same text will be mixed up incorrectly. AKV is built on SGLang, the code is public, and a client needs to send only one extra field.

An agent working on a hard task often goes back and forth with tools such as search, web pages and code execution for hundreds of turns. On every turn the model re-reads the KV cache of everything that came before. The paper measures that reading this old cache accounts for 82.4% of total inference cost, far more than generating new tokens. The usual way to save money is to delete or summarize old messages, but any edit to earlier text invalidates all the cache after it, so everything from the edit point onward has to be recomputed. A Tsinghua team proposes working at a different layer: leave the text history untouched and drop only selected entries from the cache, while the remaining entries are reused as they are. They built an inference serving system for this, called AKV. Across three models and four agent benchmarks, a simple policy of "keep the cache of only the 12 most recent tool outputs" beats the common "summarize when the length limit is reached" approach, with a 1.7-point higher average score and 27.7% lower average cost.

1. The problem: recomputation is expensive, and cutting everything at once loses information

The longer an agent's conversation gets, the more trouble the cache causes. The first problem is cost: the cache keeps growing and is read on every turn, so storing and reading it is expensive. The second is accuracy: a model can only handle so much context reliably, and once the content taking part in computation goes past that range, quality drops noticeably.

The standard fix today is to edit the text, also called "context engineering": delete old messages or replace them with summaries. But an LLM's cache is computed in order, and each token's cache depends on everything before it. The earlier the edit, the longer the stretch that must be recomputed. So common agent frameworks wait until the length hits some limit and then summarize most of the history in one go, keeping only the last few turns, which keeps the number of recomputations low. Cutting everything at once like this easily throws away useful information from the middle turns too.

The authors start with a comparison. They run GPT-OSS-120B on the first 100 questions of BrowseComp-Plus (a QA benchmark that needs many rounds of search to answer), 4 attempts per question with at most 100 turns. Keeping only the 12 most recent tool outputs by deleting text every turn costs 1.85 times as much as doing nothing, because of repeated recomputation. Summarizing once at 48K tokens cuts cost by only about 7% and drops accuracy by 5 points. Dropping old tool outputs directly from the cache improves accuracy and cost at the same time.

2. Method: three operations on the cache

The authors first separate two lengths. One is how long the conversation is as text. The other is how much cache actually takes part in later computation, which the paper calls the "active cache". Text editing changes the first; cache editing changes only the second.

In this framing, the paper defines three operations:

  • Append: the normal case. Read in new tokens, attach their cache at the end, and increment the position index.
  • Drop: exclude specified cache entries from all later computation. The remaining entries stay exactly as they are, the text history is unchanged, and new tokens keep counting positions upward as usual.
  • Reposition: renumber the retained entries 0, 1, 2… in their original order, and number the next new token after them.

Why is the third operation needed? Dropping does not make the position indices smaller. The cache shrinks, but the index keeps climbing and will eventually exceed the largest position the model can handle. Repositioning pulls the indices back down. For models that use RoPE this step is cheap: to move an entry from position p to position q, rotate its key by the angle for q−p; the value stays the same and nothing is recomputed.

What gets dropped? The authors looked at the model's attention distribution and found two patterns: older content receives less attention, and at similar distances tool outputs receive less attention than the model's own reasoning. So the main policy is rolling drop of old tool outputs: keep all reasoning content and the 12 most recent tool outputs, and drop the cache of earlier tool outputs step by step.

3. The difficulty: the same text can have different caches

In a normal inference server, the same text prefix means the same cache, so caches can be reused by matching prefixes. Cache editing breaks this: the same text, reached through a different order of operations, yields a different cache.

Take the example in the figure. All three paths end with only B and C kept. But in ①, C was computed while A was still visible, so it carries A's influence. In ②, A had already been dropped when C was computed. In ③, there was no A before B even when B itself was computed. So C's cache differs across the three paths. The paper therefore describes a cache state by "the full sequence of operations applied since an empty cache": for a given model, that sequence uniquely determines the current cache. The inference server has to remember both the text history and the operation history to reuse cache correctly.

4. AKV: turning this into an inference service

AKV's interface is almost identical to a standard chat API. The client sends the full message list as usual, with one extra optional field that says "after message N, drop these entries and reposition here". The client does not need to know which caches the server still holds; each turn it just appends messages and operations as usual.

Inside the server there are three mechanisms.

The first is reuse. Inference servers usually do prefix caching with a radix tree, so requests with the same prefix share a segment of cache. AKV adds "drop" and "reposition" nodes to the tree and matches on both text and operations during lookup. That is why ① and ② in the figure can share the A–B segment, while each keeps its own copy of C because A was dropped at different times.

The second is reclamation. A cache entry can be freed only when no in-flight computation still needs it. For example, once both ① and ② have dropped A, A's cache can be freed without waiting for the requests to finish. When GPU memory is tight, the server first reclaims cache that has been dropped and only then cache from finished requests, because the latter is more likely to be needed next turn.

The third is recovery. Once cache has been evicted from GPU memory, it has to be recomputed the next time it is needed. But a normal recompute from scratch can only produce the cache of "nothing ever dropped", and replaying each operation step by step would take many passes. AKV instead splits the content to be recomputed, at each layer, into segments at the drop and reposition points. Each segment attends only to itself and to the cache that earlier segments still retained at that time, and all segments are computed in one pass. This way a single computation restores the exact state after the drops and repositions.

5. Results

The baselines are two "summarize at the limit" approaches. The "standard" approach uses each model's own higher limit (96K tokens for GPT-OSS-120B and MiniMax-M2.7, 192K for MiroThinker-1.7-Mini). The "text editing" approach uses the same summarization but lowers the limit to 48K for all models. AKV uses rolling drop with "keep the 12 most recent tool outputs". There are four benchmarks: two multi-round search QA sets (BrowseComp-Plus, xbench-DeepSearch), the 103 text-only questions of GAIA, and SWE-bench Verified, which fixes bugs in real code repositories. Cost is priced on tokens actually read and generated. To avoid favoring their own method, the authors also charge every token touched by repositioning at the cache-read price, deliberately overestimating the cost of that step.

Average over the four benchmarks (score is pass rate %, cost is cents per task):

ModelStandardText editingAKV
MiniMax-M2.752.4 pts / 5.0 cents52.8 / 5.753.7 / 4.4
GPT-OSS-120B51.0 / 11.248.3 / 10.253.1 / 7.3
MiroThinker-1.7-Mini44.1 / 20.437.1 / 18.145.8 / 14.8

On all three models AKV has the highest average score, and its average cost is 27.7% lower than the standard approach and 21.9% lower than text editing. It does not win every cell, though: on MiniMax-M2.7, text editing scores higher on BrowseComp-Plus, and the standard approach is slightly higher on SWE-bench.

Why does accuracy improve? The authors break the results down by conversation length. Below 48K tokens the three approaches are about the same; between 48K and 96K, text editing is worst; above 96K, the standard approach is worst. These are exactly the points where each one triggers summarization, which shows that the lost points come from information thrown away by cutting everything at once. Rolling drop removes the oldest tool outputs a little at a time, so it avoids this problem.

On speed, the authors measure serving efficiency on SWE-bench with 8 A800 GPUs. At the highest concurrency each system can sustain, AKV's average latency is 1.36 times faster, the slowest 5% of requests are 1.51 times faster, and output throughput is 1.18 times that of the standard approach. The gap widens as concurrency goes up: the standard approach runs short of GPU memory and keeps evicting and recomputing cache, so at concurrency 16 the slowest 5% of requests wait 230 seconds, versus 31 seconds for AKV.

Several ablations are also useful. Dropping without repositioning scores 55.0 on BrowseComp-Plus; adding repositioning raises it to 62.0, because the agent can keep searching instead of hitting the position limit and being forced to stop. Dropping the cache of reasoning content, alone or together with tool outputs, is worse than dropping only tool outputs. The authors also tried letting the agent decide what to drop, and two models reached 61.0% and 64.0% on a subset of BrowseComp-Plus, which suggests the policy itself still has a lot of room to explore.

6. Limitations and practical value

The limitations the authors list: what to drop and when still needs more exploration; agents have not yet been trained specifically under this mechanism; and models with newer architectures such as linear attention are not supported. Dropped content still leaves an indirect influence through cache computed afterwards. The authors see this as a strength, but it also means results depend on the order of operations, so debugging and reproduction require recording the full operation sequence.

papers.title: Stratified Sparse Attention: Reducing the Sparse-to-Dense Gap at Extreme Sparsity
papers.abstract: Large Language Model inference over long contexts is increasingly bottlenecked by the cost of attending to a growing Key-Value (KV) cache. Sparse attention reduces this cost by accessing only a fraction of the cache, but existing methods face a trade-off between deterministic retrieval, which captures high-scoring tokens but discards residual attention mass, and sampling, which improves coverage at the cost of higher variance. Hybrid methods combine top-$k$ retrieval with uniform sampling, yet still exhibit a substantial gap from dense attention at aggressive sparsity. We introduce \emph{Stratified Sparse Attention (SSA)}, a unified framework combining deterministic retrieval with score-guided sampling. SSA deterministically attends to high-scoring tokens while sampling the residual using proxy attention scores and correcting for their inclusion probabilities, thereby recovering attention mass beyond the retrieval set. SSA encompasses top-$k$, top-$p$, and hybrid top-$k$+sampling as special cases. Across RULER, LongBench, LOFT, and AIME, and five models ranging from 3B to 27B parameters, SSA consistently improves over the baselines at matched sparsity. On RULER-HARD with Ministral-3-8B, SSA improves accuracy over the strongest practical baseline from 81.8\% to 84.2\% at 32K and from 63.8\% to 69.3\% at 128K under $50\times$ attention sparsity, recovering 94\% and 85\% of dense-attention performance, respectively. With optimized CUDA kernels, SSA achieves up to $2.96\times$ decode speedup over FlashInfer at 1M context, demonstrating that its accuracy gains translate into practical long-context inference acceleration. We open-source our code at https://github.com/skylight-org/SSA-Paper-Code.
papers.authors: Sahil Joshi, Prithvi Dixit, Aryan Katiyar, Agniva Chowdhury, Joseph E. Gonzalez, Anshumali Shrivastava, Aditya Desai, Kumar Krishna Agrawal
